annotations.title: Jesus Christ
annotations.short: Forty days without food. Jesus Christ sits alone, his chin in his hand.
annotations.extended: Mark’s Gospel gives the scene two short verses: after his baptism, Christ was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, while angels served him. Moretto shows no struggle. Christ rests his head on his hand, a gesture long used in art for meditation and for melancholy.

more.story: He is hungry and tired, as any man would be. Yet around him the wild animals lie still.

verses.text: You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor.
But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor

annotations.title: The Angels
annotations.short: Two angels come down from the upper right to serve him.
annotations.extended: Mark and Matthew both end the wilderness story with angels attending Christ. Here two of them arrive in flight from the upper right.

more.story: Satan quoted the psalm about angels and told him to jump from the Temple. He refused. Afterward the angels came anyway.

verses.text: For He will command His angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.
Then the devil left Him, and angels came and ministered to Him.

annotations.title: The Basilisk
annotations.short: A small winged serpent, half hidden near the center. It may be a basilisk.
annotations.extended: The creature is not named in the Met’s record; reading it as a basilisk is an interpretation. If it is one, it points to Psalm 91, which Satan quotes to Christ during the temptation. The next verse in the Latin Bible of Moretto’s day reads, in an early English translation: “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk: and thou shalt trample under foot the lion and the dragon.”

more.story: In the Latin Bible Moretto knew, the psalm Satan quoted goes on to put the basilisk under foot. Here it crouches low near Jesus Christ.

verses.text: Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk: and thou shalt trample under foot the lion and the dragon.
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.

annotations.title: The Lion
annotations.short: The lion lies at his feet, head lowered, half outside the picture.
annotations.extended: Lions are among the wild beasts the Met identifies in the painting. In Christian art the lion can stand for strength and kingship, and the same verse of Psalm 91 that names the basilisk promises that the lion will be trampled. Here it is calm, which suits a reading of the wilderness as a place where creation is at peace with Christ.

more.story: God sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths for Daniel. This lion needs no angel; it lies down before Jesus Christ.

verses.text: My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.
Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed

annotations.title: The Stag
annotations.short: A stag at the left stretches forward, its head lowered toward him.
annotations.extended: A stag crosses the slope at the left. The deer was a familiar Christian image of the soul seeking God, taken from Psalm 42. Whether Moretto meant that here, or simply painted the animals of a wild place, cannot be settled from the picture alone.

more.story: The deer is not one of the dangerous ones. Christians have long seen it as the soul, thirsty for God.

verses.text: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God.
If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.

annotations.title: The Fox
annotations.short: A fox rests a few steps from the serpent.
annotations.extended: The Met’s catalogue lists foxes among the painting’s animals. No single symbolic meaning fits them securely here; they belong, with the bear and the deer, to the wild beasts Mark says were with Christ.

more.story: Every animal on this hillside has a den or a nest. The one through whom they were made has nowhere to lay his head.

verses.text: Through Him all things were made
Foxes have dens… but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.

annotations.title: The Bear
annotations.short: A bear lies in the grass, head down, as quiet as the rest.
annotations.extended: The Met’s catalogue lists a bear among the painting’s animals. Predators lying at rest near grazing animals recall Isaiah’s peaceable kingdom, where the wolf lives with the lamb and the bear feeds beside the cow. That echo is a reading, not something the painting states.

more.story: Alone in these hills, a man would fear a bear. Beside Jesus Christ it lies down as calmly as the cow in Isaiah’s vision.

verses.text: The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together
He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.

annotations.title: The Missing Picture
annotations.short: Faint cherubs at the left edge, where the original canvas was cut down.
annotations.extended: The Met describes the canvas as a fragment of a larger work that once continued past the sketchy cherubim at the left and showed other events from Christ’s life. It has been suggested that Moretto’s Christ Blessing Saint John the Baptist, now in London, came from the same composition, though the National Gallery notes that the figures differ in scale.

more.story: Moretto’s painting once continued past this edge, with other scenes from the life of Jesus Christ.

verses.text: There are many more things that Jesus did.
